sections.heading: Dialogue III, Knot xv (printed pp. 394–401)
rows: Andab. Verum, ais in causis a priori contineri ut ad hoc singulare sese determinet?
Andab. But, do you say [that] it is contained in the causes a priori [a priori] that it should determine itself to this singular [thing]?
[Margin, p. 394: Nodus XV. Libertatem non repugnare providentiae.]
[Margin, p. 394: Knot XV. That liberty is not repugnant [repugnare] to providence.]

Ereu. Aio equidem, sed non sic ut ipsi eum determinent, sed ut faciant eum sese determinare. Si vero hoc petis, ut, quoniam dicitur sese determinare, idcirco debeat prima quaedam & originalis esse, ita ut nulla sit ea prior; manifeste falsum & absurdum petis. Falsum, quia videmus nos infinitis agentibus & ex parte nos moventibus undique obsideri: Absurdum vero quia causae quam secundariam ipsemet agnoscis, hoc vis tribuere, ut a nullo pendeat.

Ereu. I say [so] indeed, but not so that they themselves determine him, but so that they make him determine himself. But if you ask [petis] this, that, since it is said to determine itself, therefore it must be a certain first and original [cause], so that none be prior to it [ea]; you ask [a thing] manifestly false and absurd. False, because we see ourselves to be besieged on every side by infinite agents, and [agents] moving us in part [ex parte]: but absurd, because to a cause which you yourself acknowledge [to be] secondary, you wish to attribute this, that it depend on none.

Andab. Undecumque sive pendet sive non pendet, hoc ei debet concedi ut possit agere, & non agere; si autem ab aliquibus quibuscumque causis iam determinatum sit ei ut hoc agat, non potest non hoc agere. Ergo iam non est libera. Arguo enim sic. Non potest agere illud quod non potest agi. Sed aliud quam quod agit non potest agi, ergo homo non potest illud agere. Subsumptum sic confirmo. Eo ipso quod praedefinitum sit sive in causa prima, sive in serie secundarum quod unum singulare agetur, praefinitum etiam est quod alia non agentur, sed quod praefinitum est non fore, non impossibile est ut sit: Impossibile itaque est ut aliud agatur, vel per consequens ut homo aliud agat. Non potest itaque non agere quod acturus est.

Andab. From wherever it either depends or does not depend, this must be granted to it, that it be able to act, and not to act; but if by any causes whatever it has already been determined for it that it should do [agat] this, it cannot not do this. Therefore it is now not free. For I argue thus. It cannot do that which cannot be done. But [anything] other than what it does cannot be done, therefore man cannot do that. The subsumption [subsumptum] I confirm thus. By the very fact that it has been predefined [praedefinitum], either in the first cause, or in the series of secondary [causes], that one singular [thing] will be done, it has also been prefined [praefinitum] that other [things] will not be done; but what has been prefined not to be going to be [non fore], it is not impossible [sic] that it be: It is impossible therefore that another [thing] be done, or by consequence that man do another [thing]. He cannot therefore not do what he is about to do [acturus est].

Ereu. Et non legisti multa futura esse quae non erunt? & quod maiori ratione nititur, multa posse fieri quae non fient? si vero tua ratiocinatio perfecta foret, nihil fieri posset quod non etiam ipsum futurum sit. Ut, si argumentum tibi ipse repetere velis, sine me videbis. Noveris itaque te rem a natura ad Logicam & voces revocavisse, ut iam quaestio sit, quot significationibus accipi possit τὸ posse fieri vel facere. Et ostendendum quomodo in una significatione acceptum non repugnet consistere cum impossibili, in alia rursus significatione usurpato.

Ereu. And have you not read that many [things] are future [futura] which will not be? and, what rests [nititur] on greater reason, that many [things] can come to be which will not come to be? but if your reasoning [ratiocinatio] were perfect, nothing could come to be which also itself were not future. As, if you wish yourself to repeat the argument to yourself, you will see without me. You should know [noveris] therefore that you have called the matter [rem] back from nature to Logic and to words [voces], so that now the question is, in how many significations the [τὸ] ‘can come to be’ [posse fieri] or ‘[can] make’ [facere] can be taken. And it must be shown how, taken in one signification, it is not repugnant [that it] consist with the impossible, [the impossible being] used [usurpato] again in another signification.

Age igitur non vides quaedam sive entia sive qualitates nomen potentiarum obtinere; ut serra, securis, culter potentiam secandi habent, pedes ambulandi, manus apprehendendi vel tangendi, oculi videndi, &c. Vides itaque quaedam ex essentiis suis habere ut dicantur posse tale vel tale quippiam. Hoc tibi considerandum ex una parte propone.

Come then, do you not see that certain either beings [entia] or qualities obtain the name of potencies [potentiarum]; as a saw, an axe, a knife have the potency [potentiam] of cutting, feet of walking, hands of grasping or touching, eyes of seeing, etc. You see therefore that certain [things] have from their essences that they are said to be able [posse] [to do] such or such a something. This propose to yourself to be considered on the one part.

Ex alia vero vide Logicos definientes possibile illud esse, quo posito nullum sequitur inconveniens. Incommodum autem sequi potest vel ab intrinseco, vel ab accidenti aliquo. Vides itaque duas species possibiles, seu magis duo significata vocis. Unum est ut illud sit possibile ad quod est potentia, alterum vero ut illud sit possibile, ad quod non modo sit potentia; sed etiam ea in iis circumstantiis collocata sit, ut nullum sit incommodum si haec potentia exeat in actum.

But on the other, see the Logicians defining the possible to be that which being posited, no inconvenient [thing] [inconveniens] follows. But an inconvenience [incommodum] can follow either from [something] intrinsic, or from some accident. You see therefore two possible species, or rather two significations [significata] of the word [vocis]. One is that that be possible to which there is a potency [potentia], but the other that that be possible, to which not only there be a potency, but also it [the potency] be placed in those circumstances, that there be no inconvenience if this potency go out into act [exeat in actum].

Nunc attende quomodo libertas dicatur potentia, priori vel posteriori modo: Et cum palam sit esse hominis vel mentis qualitatem, pariter expeditum est eam primo modo dici; & cum dicitur posse plura, dici, per naturam suam essentialem & intrinsecam ea posse. Vide ex alia parte tuum argumentum, & quomodo naturam possibilis accipias, & videbis te in posteriori significatione ea uti. Evidentissimum itaque est, argumentum tuum declarata aequivocatione laborare.

Now attend how liberty is called a potency, in the prior or the posterior mode: And since it is plain [that it] is a quality of the man or of the mind, equally it is clear [expeditum] that it is called [so] in the first mode; and when it is said to be able [to do] several [things] [posse plura], [that] it is said to be able [to do] them through its essential and intrinsic nature. See on the other part your argument, and how you take the nature of the possible, and you will see that you use it [ea] in the posterior signification. It is most evident therefore that your argument labours under the declared equivocation [aequivocatione].

Ergo cum dicis non potest agere illud quod non potest agi, hoc laboras, non posse per sua essentialia illud quod per accidens effici negatur, quod falsum est. Etsi enim praedefinitione impossibile redditum quidpiam sit, hoc non tollit neque minuit intrinsecam potestatem agentis in qua consistit immota & integra libertas hominis.

Therefore when you say ‘it cannot do that which cannot be done’, you labour [to prove] this, that [a thing] cannot through its essentials [do] that which by accident [per accidens] is denied to be effected; which is false. For even if something has been rendered impossible by predefinition [praedefinitione], this does not take away nor diminish the intrinsic power [potestatem] of the agent, in which consists, unmoved and entire, the liberty of man.

Verum iam dispicio nihil tibi facturum satis, nisi ipsam quam tu ingrederis, semitam impossibilem ostendero. Est itaque plurium assertio, cui te favere credo, libertatem in eo sitam esse, ut homo postquam in utramque partem proposita sibi libraverit, ex mero motu voluntatis in alteram resideat partem, praecise quia vult. In quo, quot sint incommoda vide.

But now I discern [that] nothing will satisfy [facturum satis] you, unless I shall have shown the very path which you enter upon [to be] impossible. It is therefore the assertion of the many [plurium], which I believe you favour, that liberty is placed in this, that a man, after he has weighed [libraverit] on either side [the things] proposed to him, out of the mere motion of the will settles [resideat] on one [alteram] side, precisely because he wills. In which, see how many inconveniences [incommoda] there are.

Primo omnem experientiam tollis & communem sensum hominum: nam & coniectare possunt homines quid alius acturus sit, & rationes ad persuadendum adhibent, & expectant moveri hominem a similibus rationibus: quae, si verum est voluntatem a ratione non moveri, sed ad proposita ex mera sua inclinatione & non ex momentis propositorum flecti, prorsus vana & omni ratione destituta sunt. Rursus tollitur omnis prudentia, & natura rationalis ab homine. Si enim electio hominis non praeponderat in eam partem quo cum rationis motiva impellunt, non ex ratione agit neque natus est a prudentia gubernari, sed mero casu & fortuna.

First, you take away all experience and the common sense of men: for both men can conjecture what another is about to do, and they apply reasons [rationes] for persuading, and they expect a man to be moved by like reasons: which [things], if it is true that the will is not moved by reason, but is bent to [the things] proposed out of its mere inclination and not out of the moments [momentis] of the [things] proposed, are utterly vain and destitute of all reason. Again, all prudence is taken away, and the rational nature, from man. For if the choice [electio] of man does not preponderate to that side whither, when [cum] the motives [motiva] of reason impel [it], he does not act out of reason nor is he born to be governed by prudence, but by mere chance and fortune.

Rursus in hac sententia nihil est in ipsa voluntate prius electione & servato actu, quo determinetur ad ipsum secundum actum, id est, ad utrum duorum propositorum sese porrigat. Ego [sic; read Ergo] ut hoc magis illo acceptet, causam nullam habet. Vides itaque primo huic principio (nihil esse sine causa) libertatis tuae notionem intrinsecus repugnare.

Again, in this opinion there is nothing in the will itself prior to the choice, and with the act kept [servato actu], by which it may be determined to the second act itself, that is, to which of the two [things] proposed it should stretch itself. [Therefore] that it accept this rather than that, it has no cause. You see therefore, first, that to this principle (that nothing is without a cause) the notion of your liberty is intrinsically repugnant.

Repugnat etiam virtutum habitibus. Omnes enim habitus & maxime virtutum hoc habent, ut non tantum ex iis sequatur hominem posse, sed secundum earum modum etiam velle & facere illud ad quod inclinant: At si voluntatis determinatio nullam priorem causam habeat, hoc impossibile erit.

It is repugnant also to the habits [habitibus] of the virtues. For all habits, and most of all [those] of the virtues, have this, that not only does it follow from them that a man is able, but [that] according to their mode [he] also wills and does that to which they incline: But if the determination of the will has no prior cause, this will be impossible.

Tandem ipsi primae causae iniuria fit. Ponitur enim haec determinatio voluntatis tam absoluta, ut neque a Deo pendeat, quantum ad ipsam speciem: si enim penderet; iam in Deo praehaberetur quo versus sese inclinatura foret. Immo praevenit ipsam cognitionem Dei, ut eam neque cognoscere possit, nisi ex suppositione quod futura sit, & quasi ex ipsa iam actu. Neque tam cito crediderim te oblitum quomodo Asphalius demonstraverit futuritionem effectus, nisi ex Deo pendeat, fatalitatem absolutam & Stoicam inferre. Vide quantis incommodis implicetur illa sententia.

Finally, injury is done to the first cause itself. For this determination of the will is posited so absolute, that it does not depend on God, as far as regards the species [speciem] itself: for if it depended, already it would be pre-had [praehaberetur] in God whither it would be about to incline itself. Nay, it forestalls [praevenit] the very knowledge of God, so that He could not even know it, except from the supposition that it is future, and as it were from it already in act. Nor would I believe you so quickly forgetful how Asphalius demonstrated that the futurition [futuritionem] of an effect, unless it depend on God, infers an absolute and Stoic fatality [fatalitatem]. See in how great inconveniences that opinion is entangled.
Asphal. Unde igitur tot excellentia ingenia in eam propendent, & quasi irrefragabilem habent?
Asphal. Whence then do so many excellent wits [ingenia] lean towards it, and hold [it] as it were irrefragable?

Ereu. Vide modum nostrum concipiendi, quomodo a rebus differt: [Margin, p. 399: Exercitium libertatis esse motum.] hoc quod est aedificare diebus, & mensibus, & annis totis exercetur; nos unico verbo (aedificavit) quasi in instanti consummamus. Hoc quod est calefacere, subiecto & refecto igne, longo tempore ad actum reducitur, per non interpolatum motum, & idem in dealbare, denigrare, &c. fit: quae tamen nos unico verbo comprehendimus:

Ereu. See our mode of conceiving, how it differs from things: [Margin, p. 399: That the exercise of liberty is a motion.] this which is ‘to build’ is exercised in days, and months, and whole years; we with a single word (‘he built’) consummate [it] as it were in an instant. This which is ‘to heat’, the fire being put under and renewed [refecto], is brought to act over a long time, through an uninterrupted [non interpolatum] motion, and the same comes about in ‘to whiten’, ‘to blacken’, etc.: which nevertheless we comprehend with a single word:

hinc fit ut qui ad verba & notiones nostras magis quam ad naturam rerum attenti sunt (ut fere sunt quos lites Logicae delectant) facile in eum delabantur errorem, ut etiam rem ipsam indivisibiliter perfici existiment, motum autem non esse nisi dispositionum introductionem credant. Hinc formae albedinis, caloris, aedificii & cathedrae, &c. quasi indivisibiliter finito motu creduntur influi.

hence it comes about that those who are attentive to our words and notions more than to the nature of things (as for the most part are those whom Logical quarrels [lites] delight) easily slip down into that error, that they think even the thing itself to be perfected indivisibly, and believe motion to be nothing but the introduction of dispositions. Hence the forms of whiteness, of heat, of a building and of a chair, etc. are believed to be flowed in [influi] as it were indivisibly, the motion being finished.

Hinc etiam homines non advertentes libertatis actum seu deliberationem motum quendam esse, quo paulatim homo ex indeterminato fit determinatus, putaverunt totam consultationem esse solummodo conditionem; in ipso vero ultimo instanti totam determinationis notitiam & rationem contineri: atque adeo nihil extra illam considerantes putaverunt necessarium esse ut voluntas in ipso instanti suae determinationis (si abstracte consideretur ab ipsa determinatione vel actu suo) debere nondum includere unde determinate procedat ad opus, sed in plena sua indifferentia consistere.

Hence also men, not adverting that the act of liberty, or deliberation, is a certain motion, by which little by little a man from undetermined becomes determined, thought the whole consultation [consultationem] to be only a condition; but in the last instant itself the whole notion [notitiam] and reason [rationem] of the determination to be contained: and so, considering nothing outside that [instant], they thought it necessary that the will, in the very instant of its determination (if it be considered abstractly from the determination itself or its act), ought [debere] not yet to include whence it may proceed determinately to the work, but to stand [consistere] in its full indifference.

Quod si verum foret, frustra natura toto illo priori intervallo desudavisset, cum nihil amplius ad finem suum effecisset, quam si nudam partium propositionem (quam in primo instanti perfecerat) reliquisset.

Which if it were true, in vain would nature have sweated through that whole prior interval, since she would have effected nothing more towards her end than if she had left the bare proposition of the sides [partium] (which she had completed in the first instant).

Andab. Sed hoc etiam te videre par est, Ereuni, tuam aeque sententiam contra ea principia peccare, quae tu per se nota existimas. Fateris enim voluntatem ab ipsa se moveri, cum tamen idem in semetipsum agere posse impossibile reputes.

Andab. But it is fair [par est] that you see this also, Ereunius, that your opinion equally sins against those principles which you esteem known through themselves [per se nota]. For you confess that the will is moved by itself, while nevertheless you reckon it impossible that the same can act upon itself.

Ereu. Eodem ergo etiamnum errore laberis quem explicabam. [Margin, p. 400: Voluntatem non immediate movere semetipsam.] Ex eo enim quod dixerim voluntatem in semetipsam agere, statim suscipis immediate in semetipsam operari. Quod non sic se habet.

Ereu. Then you are still slipping in the same error which I was explaining. [Margin, p. 400: That the will does not immediately move itself.] For from this, that I have said that the will acts upon itself, you at once take [it] up [suscipis] [that it] operates immediately upon itself. Which is not so.

Sed cum (quod ipse optime nosti) partes diversae eiusdem corporis plurium corporum rationem induant, si diversis sint instructae qualitatibus & virtutibus, fit ut voluntas per unam partem corporis agat in aliam, per quam aliam reflectatur motus in ipsammet rursus voluntatem: verbi causa, voluntas movendo passionem aliquam circa cor, immittit spiritus cerebro qui certas species commoveant, a quibus pulsetur aestimativa, quae rursus in voluntatem motum refundat. Unde vides nihil in hoc sui motu esse quod principio illi per se moto vim aliquam valeat inferre.

But since (which you yourself know very well) diverse parts of the same body put on the reason [rationem] of several bodies, if they be furnished with diverse qualities and virtues [virtutibus], it comes about that the will through one part of the body acts on another, through which other the motion is reflected again into the will itself: for example [verbi causa], the will, by moving some passion about the heart, sends spirits [spiritus] into the brain, which stir up certain species [species], by which the estimative [aestimativa] is struck, which pours back the motion again into the will. Whence you see [that] there is nothing in this its [sui] motion which could [valeat] bring any force [vim] upon that principle moved [moto; ?read noto, ‘known’] through itself.

Asphal. Incipio tui misereri, Ereuni, quo enim plura nobis expedis, eo etiam plura manum tuam requirere videntur. Ecce enim ex eo quod nos docuisti Deum esse mundi huius gubernatorem, neque posse non optimum facere, finem quoque mundi vel huius certe quem calcamus orbis, esse hominem: clare sequitur, tunc orbem optime gubernari, si secundum finem suum, hoc est generis humani usum & opus gubernetur. Hoc modo quantas patitur calumnias non ignoras, ut quantus tibi supersit labor ipse indoleam.

Asphal. I begin to pity you, Ereunius, for the more [things] you clear up [expedis] for us, by so much the more [things] seem to require your hand. For behold, from this, that you have taught us that God is the governor of this world, and cannot not do the best, [and] that the end also of the world, or at any rate [certe] of this globe [orbis] which we tread, is man: it clearly follows that the globe is then governed best, if it be governed according to its end, that is, the use and work [opus] of the human race. In this mode how great calumnies it suffers you are not ignorant, so that I myself grieve [indoleam] how great a labour remains for you.
Ereu. Dimittere me potes, cum libuerit.
Ereu. You can dismiss me, when it shall have pleased [you].

Andab. Sed non ego. Cum Asphalio enim diversaris, & liberam habet, cum voluerit, exigendi a te quod succurrerit, potestatem: Me ante solem crastinum discedere res meae cogunt, & ipse minitatus es, cum evolaveris, ex hac qua te conclusimus cavea, non facilem receptum fore. Tu ergo, Asphali, ne parcito, sed ingere quicquid habes. Pro me respondeo quod addita Iuno nusquam aberit.

Andab. But not I. For you lodge [diversaris] with Asphalius, and he has free power [potestatem], when he will, of exacting from you what shall have occurred [to him]: My affairs compel me to depart before tomorrow's sun, and you yourself have threatened [that], when you shall have flown out of this cage in which we have shut you up, there will not be an easy recapture [receptum]. You therefore, Asphalius, do not spare, but heap on whatever you have. For me I answer that ‘Juno, added [addita], will nowhere be absent’.

terms: That liberty is not repugnant [repugnare] to providence
conflict with, be incompatible with; fight against.
Title of the knot; repugnare is the scholastic term for logical incompatibility, rendered ‘be repugnant’ throughout (glossary).
beforehand; from what is prior (in the order of causes).
Scholastic sense: in the prior causes, not Kant's sense of knowledge independent of experience.
Technical logic: the minor of a syllogism (‘Sed aliud quam quod agit non potest agi’).
Terms from the De auxiliis controversy (Bañezian praedefinitio physica / decrees); glossary renderings kept.
futura … quae non erunt; non fore
future [things] which will not be; not to be going to be
futuribles / conditional futures; ‘not be about to be’.
White distinguishes ‘future’ in the sense of possible-to-come from what actually will be, the classic Aristotelian future-contingents problem (De interpretatione 9).
the ‘can come to be’ or ‘[can] make’
the term ‘to be able to happen / to do’.
Greek article τό used to quote a phrase as a term (scholastic/humanist usage).
possibile, quo posito nullum sequitur inconveniens
the possible, which being posited, no inconvenient [thing] follows
The standard logicians' definition of the possible (Aristotle, Prior Analytics I.13, 32a18–20).
Terminist logic: the significata of a vox; basis of White's charge of equivocation.
Glossary distinction kept: potentia = potency (faculty in a subject), potestas = power (intrinsic power of the agent).
by what belongs to its essence / by what is accidental.
The two senses of ‘possible’ mapped onto essence vs. accident.
balanced; comes to rest, sinks down (on one side).
Image of a balance (libra) — White's mechanical picture of deliberation; resideat = the scale coming to rest.
Physical sense of momentum (weight on a balance) applied to motives; cf. glossary momentum.
Final causes considered as moving the will (glossary motivum).
the act being preserved; (?) reading for ‘seu primo actu’ (or first act).
The printed text is odd; it seems to contrast with secundum actum (second act = the operation), so a ‘first act’ may be meant. See notes.
Aristotelian hexis: a virtue is a habit inclining to act (Nicomachean Ethics II).
the kind/specification of the act (this rather than that).
Scholastic: specificatio actus vs. exercitium; the determination to this object.
Neologistic compound: being contained in God before the act.
Refers back to Asphalius' argument (D3-N10): futurition not grounded in God would amount to Stoic fate.
Scholastic exercitium (exercise of an act) vs. specificatio.
Scholastic influxus: forms educed/infused into matter at the end of a motion — White rejects instantaneous induction.
The opponents make deliberation a mere precondition of the free act, not its cause.
The Molinist/Jesuit ‘liberty of indifference’ that White attacks.
animal spirits; sensible images; the estimative power.
Galenic animal spirits and the scholastic internal sense (vis aestimativa) — White's physiological account of the will's reflexive motion; cf. Digby, Two Treatises.
(?) misprint for per se noto, ‘known through itself’.
Andabata had invoked principles per se nota (e.g. nothing acts on itself); see notes.
Recalls D3-N13 (the earth founded for the uses of men).
enclosure (also theatre seats); retreat, getting back.
Playful image of Ereunius as a caught bird.
Juno, set [against them], will never be away.
Virgil, Aeneid 6.90–91 (nec Teucris addita Iuno / usquam aberit): Andabata casts Asphalius as the relentless Juno who will keep pursuing Ereunius.
notes: Unit: Dialogue III, Knot xv (single part). PDF pp. 405–412 = printed pp. 394–401, from Andabata's question ‘Verum, ais in causis a priori contineri…’ (p. 394, just above the margin ‘Nodus XV. Libertatem non repugnare providentiae’, following the previous knot's boundary) to Andabata's ‘…addita Iuno nusquam aberit.’ (p. 401). Offset +11 holds (running heads 394–401; signatures Ddd ij p. 395, Ddd iij p. 397, Eee p. 401). Knot XVI (margin ‘Nodus XVI. Cur res humanae videantur casu geri’) begins p. 402 = PDF 413 with Asphalius' ‘Hanc itaque non levem querelam…’.

Uncertain / suspect readings (all checked at 300 dpi, the print is clear in each case): (1) p. 395 ‘sed quod praefinitum est non fore, non impossibile est ut sit’ — the argument requires ‘impossibile est ut sit’; the ‘non’ is printed and kept, marked [sic] in the English. (2) p. 398 ‘Ego ut hoc magis illo acceptet’ — ungrammatical with habet; read as a misprint for ‘Ergo’ and translated so. (3) p. 398 ‘prius electione & servato actu’ — printed so; possibly a corruption of ‘seu primo actu’ (contrasting with secundum actum); translated literally. (4) p. 401 ‘principio illi per se moto’ — probably for ‘per se noto’ (cf. Andabata's ‘principia … per se nota’ on p. 400); translated literally with the alternative bracketed.

Interpretive choices: (a) p. 394 ‘debeat prima quaedam & originalis esse’ — feminine; taken as ‘[cause]’ (causa), consistent with ‘causae quam secundariam’ that follows. (b) p. 395 ‘vel facere’ — taken as ‘[posse] facere’. (c) p. 400 ‘necessarium esse ut voluntas … debere’ — the construction is mixed (ut + infinitive); translated literally. (d) p. 401 ‘ut quantus tibi supersit labor ipse indoleam’ — result clause with indirect question.

Verification pass: the Latin was re-read sentence by sentence against the page images and the English.
